::: {.project-lede}
Sparse ordinal categories affect both estimation and the interpretation of model fit. This research program examines two connected questions: how well fit indices distinguish correctly specified from misspecified CFA models, and how scenario-specific cutoffs can be calibrated and evaluated for false rejection and detection.
:::

## Abstract {#abstract}

Using a Monte Carlo simulation-cum-ROC framework, the study evaluates how RMSEA, SRMR, CFI, and TLI distinguish correctly specified ordinal CFA models from two forms of misspecification under sparse response categories and category collapsing. A local misspecification is represented by an omitted cross-loading, while a structural misspecification combines two correlated factors. The analysis compares WLSMV, MLR, and MLMV across sample size, loading magnitude, sparsity, number of sparse-pattern items, collapsing intensity, and a no-collapse baseline.

## Simulation Design {#simulation-design}

::: {.mini-grid}
<div><strong>Fit indices</strong><br><span>RMSEA · SRMR · CFI · TLI</span></div>
<div><strong>Estimators</strong><br><span>WLSMV · MLR · MLMV</span></div>
<div><strong>Misspecification</strong><br><span>omitted cross-loading · combined correlated factors</span></div>
<div><strong>Information conditions</strong><br><span>sample size, loadings, sparsity, sparse items, collapsing intensity</span></div>
:::

A no-collapse baseline makes it possible to separate the effect of **sparse response structure itself** from the additional information loss introduced by category collapsing. ROC analysis evaluates both overall diagnostic separation through AUC and condition-specific operating points through sensitivity and specificity.

## Key Findings {#key-findings}

- **Discrimination varied substantially across conditions.** Fit-index performance cannot be summarized well by a single universal cutoff.
- **Local misspecification was harder to detect.** Detection weakened under moderate loadings, smaller samples, and aggressive category collapsing.
- **Structural misspecification was generally easier to detect.** Performance remained strong in many conditions, with notable deterioration under extreme sparsity and aggressive collapsing.
- **Mild and moderate collapsing produced relatively small average changes from the original response scale.** The largest losses were concentrated in more aggressive collapsing and difficult information conditions.
- **A cutoff is meaningful only when the index has adequate discrimination.** The paper therefore treats ROC-derived cutoffs as condition-specific operating points rather than new universal rules.

## BRM Paper {#brm-paper}

**Liu, L.**, Liu, J., & Okech, D. (2026). *Calibrating fit-index cutoffs for sparse ordinal CFA: Scenario-specific thresholds and operating characteristics*. *Behavior Research Methods, 58*, Article 341.

[DOI / Publisher page ↗](https://doi.org/10.3758/s13428-026-03221-8){.paper-button}

Published November 4, 2026.

The companion study moves from ROC discrimination to **scenario-specific calibration of CFI, TLI, RMSEA, and SRMR cutoffs**. It uses Correct-model reference distributions at α = .05 and examines false rejection under correct specification and detection under local and severe misspecification. The simulation covers MLR, MLMV, and WLSMV estimators, sample sizes of 250, 500, and 1,000, sparse response patterns, and original versus collapsed categories.

The calibrated cutoffs depend on the design and estimator. The paper also evaluates composite fit-index rules and provides an applied illustration using six Sierra Leone household welfare items. Reproducible code, simulation outputs, supplementary results, and the de-identified illustration data are available in the [BRM OSF repository ↗](https://osf.io/ce7rm/).

## Contribution to my research program

This project anchors my work on **measurement under sparse and heterogeneous data**. The broader program studies how response sparsity, estimator choice, category collapsing, and model-fit calibration affect the quality of measurement decisions.
